items.stem: By 1949 the USSR controlled eastern Europe through Cominform, Comecon and the Red Army. Describe the methods the USSR used to control eastern Europe.
items.answer: Communist parties loyal to Moscow ruled as one-party states. Secret police such as the Stasi in East Germany watched and arrested opponents. Soviet troops were stationed in satellite states. Cominform and later the Warsaw Pact tied the states together politically and militarily. Comecon coordinated economies to serve Soviet needs. Censorship and propaganda controlled information.

items.stem: By 1949 the USSR controlled eastern Europe through Cominform, Comecon and the Red Army. Describe the effects of Soviet control on the people of eastern Europe.

items.stem: By 1949 the USSR controlled eastern Europe through Cominform, Comecon and the Red Army. ‘Military force was the main way the USSR controlled eastern Europe.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Soviet troops crushed uprisings in East Germany (1953) and Hungary (1956). The Warsaw Pact justified stationing troops in satellite states. Judgement: Force was the ultimate guarantee of control, but day-to-day control relied on communist parties, secret police and economic ties.

items.stem: In November 1956 Soviet tanks entered Budapest to crush the Hungarian Uprising. ‘The Hungarian Uprising failed because the West did not help.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Radio Free Europe broadcasts encouraged Hungarians to expect help that never came. Without Western support the rebels could not resist Soviet tanks. Against: The USSR was determined to keep Hungary in the Warsaw Pact. The Soviet army was overwhelmingly strong. Western help risked nuclear war, so it was never realistic. Nagy's move to leave the Warsaw Pact made a Soviet attack certain. Judgement: Western help could not have changed the result without risking nuclear war; the uprising failed because the USSR was determined and able to crush it.

items.stem: In June 1963 President Kennedy visited West Berlin. Describe the consequences of the Berlin Wall.
items.answer: The flood of refugees from East Germany was stopped. Families and friends were separated for decades. More than a hundred people were killed trying to cross, such as Peter Fechter in 1962. It became a symbol of the Cold War and of the lack of freedom in the East. It reduced the immediate crisis over Berlin and the risk of war.

items.answer: For: It showed communism had to imprison its own people to stop them leaving. It was a propaganda gift to the West, as shown by Kennedy's visit in 1963. Judgement: The Wall was a practical success for the USSR in controlling East Germany, but a moral and propaganda defeat that exposed the weakness of communism's appeal.

items.stem: ‘The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 was a success for the USSR.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Communist control was restored and the reforms were ended. The Brezhnev Doctrine warned other satellites not to try reform. The West did not intervene. items.stem: Describe the rise of Solidarity in Poland in 1980-81.
items.answer: Rising food prices led to strikes, including at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980. Strikers led by Lech Wałęsa issued 21 demands, including free trade unions and the right to strike. The government accepted the Gdańsk Agreement in August 1980. Solidarity grew to about ten million members. In December 1981 General Jaruzelski declared martial law and banned Solidarity.

items.stem: Describe the collapse of communist rule in eastern Europe in 1989.
items.answer: In Poland, Solidarity won semi-free elections in June 1989 and a non-communist Prime Minister took office. Hungary opened its border with Austria and East Germans escaped to the West. Mass protests in East Germany led to the opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November. The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia. In Romania Ceauşescu was overthrown and executed in December.

items.stem: ‘Gorbachev was the main reason for the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: He refused to use force, abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine. Glasnost encouraged open criticism. His reforms raised hopes of change in the satellites. Against: Economic failure made the communist system unsustainable. Solidarity in Poland showed communism could be challenged. People power in the satellites forced change. Western pressure and the arms race added to Soviet economic problems. Judgement: Gorbachev did not intend to end Soviet control, but his refusal to use force allowed long-standing discontent and economic failure to bring it down.

items.stem: How far did the Hungarian Uprising show that Soviet control of eastern Europe was secure? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The USSR crushed the rising in days and installed a loyal leader. The West did not intervene, showing it accepted the Soviet sphere. Against: The uprising showed deep hatred of Soviet rule. Control depended on force rather than consent. Kádár later had to allow some economic reforms to keep people content. Judgement: The rising showed that Soviet control was militarily secure but politically fragile, depending on the threat of force.

items.stem: Between 1949 and 1961 millions of East Germans left for the West, many of them through Berlin. (a) Describe the consequences of the Berlin Wall. [4] (b) ‘The Berlin Wall was a sign of Soviet weakness rather than strength.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) The flood of refugees from East Germany was stopped. Families and friends were separated for decades. More than a hundred people were killed trying to cross, such as Peter Fechter in 1962. It became a symbol of the Cold War and of the lack of freedom in the East. It reduced the immediate crisis over Berlin and the risk of war. (b) For: It showed communism had to imprison its own people to stop them leaving. It was a propaganda gift to the West, as shown by Kennedy's visit in 1963. Against: It solved the refugee problem and stabilised East Germany. The West accepted it without action. It strengthened Soviet control of East Germany for nearly 30 years. Judgement: The Wall was a practical success for the USSR in controlling East Germany, but a moral and propaganda defeat that exposed the weakness of communism's appeal.

items.stem: On the night of 20-21 August 1968 Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia. ‘The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 was a success for the USSR.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Communist control was restored and the reforms were ended. The Brezhnev Doctrine warned other satellites not to try reform. The West did not intervene. Against: The invasion damaged the USSR's reputation around the world, including among communists in the West. It showed control relied on force, not consent. Romania and Yugoslavia criticised it, exposing divisions. Judgement: In the short term it was a success, but it showed that Soviet control depended on force, a weakness exposed in the 1980s.

items.stem: Why was Solidarity a threat to Soviet control? Give one reason.
items.answer: It was an independent organisation outside Communist Party control, which was not allowed under communism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid reason, for example: It was an independent organisation outside Communist Party control, which was not allowed under communism. It had about ten million members, a large share of Poland's workers. It had the support of the Catholic Church and the Polish Pope. Other satellites might copy it. [1]

items.stem: Which of these events happened last?

items.answer: The Warsaw Pact was dissolved
items.markingKey: The Warsaw Pact was dissolved (1991); martial law was declared in Poland (1981); Gorbachev became Soviet leader (1985); the Berlin Wall was opened (1989). [1]

items.stem: In May 1955 the USSR and its satellites signed the Warsaw Pact. Why did the USSR set up the Warsaw Pact? Explain your answer.
items.answer: West Germany joined NATO in May 1955, which alarmed the USSR. It gave the USSR a legal reason to keep troops in the satellites. It tied the satellite armies to Soviet command. It was a propaganda response to NATO.

items.stem: On the night of 20-21 August 1968 Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia. How similar were the Soviet responses to Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968)? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: In both cases the USSR used tanks to crush reform. In both cases the leader was removed and a loyal communist installed. In both cases the West did not intervene. Against: Hungary's rising was violent and thousands died; resistance in Czechoslovakia was mainly non-violent. Czechoslovakia was invaded by several Warsaw Pact countries, not just the USSR. Nagy was executed; Dubček was demoted but survived. Judgement: The aim and result were very similar, but the scale of violence and the use of the Warsaw Pact were different.

items.stem: Why did Soviet control of eastern Europe collapse in 1989? Give one reason.
items.answer: Gorbachev made it clear that the USSR would not use force to keep communist governments in power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid reason, for example: Gorbachev made it clear that the USSR would not use force to keep communist governments in power. The economies of the USSR and its satellites were failing and could not match the West. Solidarity in Poland showed communism could be challenged and replaced peacefully. Glasnost allowed people to criticise their governments openly. Events in one country encouraged the next, as when Hungary opened its border. [1]
